opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me most was how quickly Greg got it. He came in with this deep intuition from language models, the idea that if you train on enough sequence data at scale, the model starts learning the underlying grammar and structure. When he looked at DNA, he saw it right away: this is just another language, arguably the oldest one, and nature has been writing in it for billions of years.

But he didn't just stay at the level of the analogy. He was incredibly hands-on. He wanted to understand the data, the tokenization questions, why you'd model at single-nucleotide resolution, how long the context needs to be to capture things like whole genomes or operons, and what the right evaluations even look like in biology. In natural language you can read the output and tell whether it's good. In biology the output is a string of A's, C's, G's and T's, and you need wet-lab experiments or very careful computational proxies to know whether the model learned anything real.

I think what he found exciting, and what I found exciting watching him, was the sense that biology is at a GPT-2-ish moment. The scaling curves are there and the models are starting to show emergent capabilities, like generating functional proteins or CRISPR systems, but we're early. There's a lot of fundamental work left, and someone with his engineering instincts could see exactly where the infrastructure and scaling lessons from AI would transfer directly. That energy, that this is a real frontier and not just an application area, was what stood out to me.

r001.rationale: The response says AI scaling lessons and infrastructure could transfer directly to biology, and connects this to modeling functional proteins and CRISPR systems.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me was how quickly he got it. Greg came in genuinely curious, not as a tourist. He sat down with the team, looked at the data, and I think what clicked for him was that the thing he'd watched happen with language, where you scale a model on a huge corpus and emergent capabilities fall out, might actually have an analog in biology.

Because the framing we had was that DNA is a language. It's the oldest language, it has a vocabulary of four letters, and evolution has been writing in it for about four billion years. So if you train a model on that corpus, across all of the tree of life, you'd expect it to pick up grammar, structure, function, the same way GPT picks up syntax and semantics from text. And Greg, having lived through the moment where that bet paid off for natural language, didn't need convincing on the premise. His questions were all about execution. How much data is there, what does the tokenization look like, where are the bottlenecks, what does the scaling curve look like.

The other thing I noticed was his willingness to just sit and do the work. He wasn't above debugging a training run or digging into why the loss curve looked the way it did. That culture, where even the most senior person is hands-on, is something we really wanted at Arc, and seeing him model it reinforced that. I also think it was useful for him to see a domain where the data isn't contaminated by the internet, where the model can't just memorize Wikipedia. Biology is a cleaner test of whether these systems actually learn something real, and I think that was part of what was compelling to him.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was how natural the idea seemed to him. In biology, we tend to focus on how complicated everything is, all the exceptions and the context you need to understand. Greg came at it from the other direction: if DNA, RNA, and proteins are sequences, and there’s an enormous amount of structure in those sequences, why wouldn’t we try to learn that structure with language models? He was very quick to see the possibility. That contrast in perspective was striking—what felt like a big conceptual leap to many biologists felt like a pretty natural next step to him.
